zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Rough Monday, warmer Thursday: the fall filament still has fuel left in the tank
subhead: Six-foot swells kept the fleet close early in the week, but the stubborn warm water off Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, and Norfolk hasn't broken yet.
body_markdown:
Grade the week a C-plus with an upward trend. Early days were a scratch — swell built to the 6-to-7-foot range with short 5-to-6 second periods, the kind of sloppy, close-together sea state that makes a long run to any of the four canyons a bad idea even before you think about fuel burn. I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated analyst behind this report — I don't own a boat, a rod, or a pair of sea boots, so I'm not out there getting tossed around in that chop myself. What I do have is buoy data, tide tables, and the accumulated chatter from boats and shops that decided to go or stay depending on how that swell behaved. This week, most smart captains stayed.

Here's the read on why that matters. The NY Bight buoy is holding water around 66°F with wave heights pushing 6.6 feet — rough enough to keep the fleet thinking hard about which canyon is worth the ride. That's the calculus every captain running Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, or Norfolk is making right now: pick the one lump or edge where the warm filament is thickest, because burning four hours of diesel into a lump that's gone lukewarm is how you turn a good trip into a bad one. The good news, and it's real news, is that the warm-water intrusion that's been parked over this stretch of the Mid-Atlantic for more than a month still hasn't cracked. That filament is the whole story right now. It's kept tuna sitting shallower than they usually do this late in September, and it's kept them meaner about eating than a typical fall pattern would suggest.

We flagged this exact setup last week — said the bite here would stay moderate as long as that warm filament kept reaching south, and it has. We also called a mixed yellowfin/mahi pattern similar to what's been showing up in the northern canyons, just a notch less stacked, and that's essentially what's playing out. Nothing about this week broke that pattern. It just got harder to fish for a few days because of the sea state, not because the fish left.

Tactically, this is a green-water/blue-water edge game. Boats that did get out worked temperature breaks and color changes along the canyon edges with a standard split spread — small spreader bars and cedar plugs on the short riggers, ballyhoo naked or skirted in bird teasers out on the long riggers, and a couple of diving swimmers in the shotgun. When yellowfin show up biting as aggressive as this pattern suggests, don't be shy about running the spread tighter than you would in peak summer — these fish have been eating out of necessity as bait gets pushed around by the warm-water edges, not out of leisure. Where the troll bite has been spotty, jigging has filled it in — vertical speed jigs in the 150-to-250 gram range worked on bait balls marked on the sounder, dropped fast and worked back up in long sweeping strokes, have accounted for a mixed bag of yellowfin and mahi under the same pieces of structure. Mahi specifically have been showing around any floating debris or weed lines that collect near the canyon edges — small stuff, chunks and short teasers with a naked ballyhoo trailer will get you a look even when the bigger fish aren't home.

Bigeye and bluefin have been quieter this week, and I'll say that plainly instead of dressing it up — the mixed reports coming back describe more incidental hookups than targeted success, mostly on the chunk after dark when boats anchored up on structure and fished butterflied bunker and squid strips soaked back on circle hooks. Wahoo have popped up on high-speed trolled Ilanders and skirted jet heads run well behind the pattern, off structure with a hard vertical relief — the kind of fish you get one bite from and then nothing for hours, so the smart approach is running that gear passively while the main spread works the tuna bite. White marlin sign has been thin — a few teased-up shots reported on dead ballyhoo with hookless teasers switched to a pitch bait, but nothing that suggests a real push yet.

Look ahead and the seas are the swing factor, not the fish. If the wind lays down through the weekend and that swell drops back into the 3-to-4 foot range, expect the fleet to spread back out across all four canyons rather than parking on whichever one is closest. That's when you'll get the clearer read on whether Spencer or Norfolk is holding the better piece of the filament — right now the data doesn't separate them cleanly, and neither should you until someone puts fresh eyes on the temperature break. The bigger clock here is the calendar. This warm-water intrusion has already outlasted its usual expiration date by weeks, and every captain running this beat knows it can't hold forever. If you've got a trip on the books in the next week to ten days, I'd treat it as borrowed time rather than a sure thing — fish it hard, work the breaks methodically, and don't assume the mahi and yellowfin will still be sitting this shallow once the first real cold front rolls through and starts pulling that filament apart.
